subject: business
title: Good Strategy, Bad Strategy: Rumelt's kernel of diagnosis, guiding policy and coherent action
dek: Most documents labelled 'strategy' are really lists of goals, slogans and hopes. In 2011 the UCLA strategy professor Richard Rumelt gave managers a sharp test for telling the difference. A good strategy, he argued, has a kernel of three parts: a diagnosis of what the real challenge is, a guiding policy for dealing with it, and a set of coherent actions that reinforce each other. Bad strategy skips the hard part, which is choosing. This lesson explains the framework first, then the four hallmarks of bad strategy, and then how Nvidia, Apple under Steve Jobs, Walmart and a small corner grocery used, or failed to use, the same logic.
era: 2007 coinage, 2011 book; cases from 1805 to the 2000s
honesty: The kernel, the four hallmarks of bad strategy and the International Harvester, DEC, 'Chad Logan', retail-bank and Nvidia examples come from Rumelt's own article 'The perils of bad strategy' (McKinsey Quarterly, June 2011), which is adapted from his book. 'Chad Logan' is Rumelt's pseudonym for a real CEO, and the DEC meeting is Rumelt's simplified retelling with three invented names. The Apple account and the corner-grocery example are taken from Virginia Postrel's Bloomberg View column on the book (August 2011) and published excerpts. These are Rumelt's interpretations, written with hindsight; other historians of Apple or Nvidia would stress other causes, such as luck, timing and technology shifts.

sections.title: Why a new definition was needed

blocks.text: By the 2000s, strategy had two very different meanings in business. In the academic and consulting world, built on Michael Porter's five forces and value chain, strategy meant a specific argument about how a firm would compete. In everyday corporate life, however, 'strategy' had become the name for an annual planning document. That document usually opened with a vision, a mission and a list of values, and then listed goals such as growing revenue by a certain percentage. Rumelt called this template-style planning, and he noticed that schools, city governments and national-security agencies had adopted it as eagerly as companies had.

Richard Rumelt, a professor at UCLA's Anderson School of Management who had also worked as a consultant, first used the phrase 'bad strategy' in 2007 at a seminar in Washington, DC, on national-security strategy. He had been invited to describe how seriously businesses approached strategy. Instead he told the audience that, in his experience, bad strategy was spreading. Over the following years he refined the idea with senior executives, and in 2011 he published it in McKinsey Quarterly and in the book Good Strategy/Bad Strategy: The Difference and Why It Matters.

His starting point was simple. A strategy is a way through a difficulty. If you cannot name the difficulty, you cannot judge whether a strategy is good, and you cannot improve it. Ambition, vision and hard work all matter, but they are not substitutes for an argument about how to overcome a specific obstacle.

sections.title: The kernel: diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent actions

blocks.text: Rumelt says every good strategy contains a kernel with three parts. The order matters, because each part depends on the one before it.

items: Diagnosis: an explanation of the nature of the challenge. A good diagnosis simplifies an overwhelming situation by deciding which few aspects are critical. It answers the question 'What is really going on here?'

Guiding policy: an overall approach chosen to cope with or overcome the obstacles named in the diagnosis. It is not a goal. It tells people which kinds of action are in and which are out, much like a signpost rather than a destination.

Coherent actions: concrete steps that are coordinated with one another so that they support the guiding policy. Rumelt insists these are not mere 'implementation details'. They are where the strategy actually does its work, and they should reinforce each other rather than pull in different directions.

blocks.text: Two ideas sit behind the kernel. The first is leverage. Good strategy finds one or two pivot points in a situation where concentrated effort produces a much larger effect, and then puts resources there. The second is choice. Because resources are limited, choosing one path means giving up others. Rumelt's line, quoted by Virginia Postrel in Bloomberg View, is that strategy is scarcity's child: to have a strategy rather than vague aspirations is to choose one path and turn away from the rest.

He illustrates the whole kernel with the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805. The British admiral Horatio Nelson was outnumbered by a combined French and Spanish fleet. The usual tactic was for two fleets to sail in parallel lines and fire broadsides. Nelson's diagnosis was that the enemy gunners were less experienced and would struggle in the heavy swell that day. His guiding policy was to break the enemy line and turn the battle into a close melee where British experience would count. The coherent actions were to split his fleet into two columns and drive them straight into the enemy line, accepting great risk for the lead ships. According to Rumelt, the French and Spanish lost 22 ships and the British lost none, although Nelson himself was killed.

sections.title: Four hallmarks, and why they keep appearing

blocks.text: Rumelt condensed bad strategy into four hallmarks. The first is failure to face the challenge. In July 1979 International Harvester produced a detailed corporate strategic plan built from five divisional plans. It projected that the company's share of agricultural equipment would rise from 16 to 20 percent and drew a profit forecast shaped like a hockey stick. It did not mention the company's grossly inefficient factories or its labour relations, which Rumelt calls the worst in US industry, even though those were why its profit margin had long been about half of its rivals'. After a long strike the company declined, sold its agricultural business to Tenneco, and what remained became the truck maker Navistar.

The second hallmark is mistaking goals for strategy. Rumelt describes a CEO he calls Chad Logan, who ran a graphic-arts company and had a '20/20 plan': 20 percent annual revenue growth and a profit margin of at least 20 percent. When Rumelt asked what strength or industry change would make that possible, Logan answered with the will to win and a quotation from Jack Welch about reaching for the impossible. Rumelt points out that Welch also said that if you do not have a competitive advantage, you should not compete. A goal tells people where you want to end up. It does not tell them how to get past the obstacle in the way.

The third hallmark is bad strategic objectives. One version is the 'dog's dinner', a long list of things to do produced by collecting every stakeholder's wishes. Rumelt met the mayor of a small city in the Pacific Northwest whose plan contained 47 strategies and 178 action items. The other version is the 'blue-sky' objective, which simply restates the desired outcome and is just as hard to achieve as the original challenge. Good objectives, by contrast, are few, pivotal and reachable with the resources the organization actually has.

The fourth hallmark is fluff: buzzwords that dress up the obvious. Rumelt quotes a retail bank whose internal memo said its fundamental strategy was 'customer-centric intermediation'. Intermediation means taking deposits and lending them out. Remove the jargon, and the sentence says that the bank's strategy is to be a bank.

Why is bad strategy so common? Rumelt gives two main reasons. One is the inability to choose. At a 1992 meeting of senior executives at Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC), one group wanted to keep building integrated computer systems, a second wanted to sell customer 'solutions', and a third wanted to focus on chips. Chief executive Ken Olsen asked them to reach consensus, but each option was preferred by a majority over one of the others, a cycle known as Condorcet's paradox. They settled on a statement that DEC was committed to high-quality products and services and to being a leader in data processing. That was a political compromise, not a strategy. Olsen was replaced in June 1992 by Robert Palmer, who chose chips, but by then it was too late. Compaq bought DEC in 1998. The other reason is template-style planning, the habit of filling in vision, mission, values and 'strategies' that are really aspirations.

sections.title: How Nvidia, Apple, Walmart and a corner grocery used the kernel

blocks.text: Nvidia is Rumelt's main worked example. The company's first product, a PC add-in board combining video, audio and 3-D graphics, was a commercial failure. In 1995 the start-up 3dfx Interactive took the lead in fast 3-D chips for gamers, and there were rumours that Intel would enter the market too. Rumelt's summary of the diagnosis is: 'We are losing the performance race.' Jensen Huang's guiding policy was to release a faster, better chip every six months instead of the industry's usual eighteen months. The coherent actions made that cycle possible: three development teams working on overlapping schedules, heavy investment in simulation and emulation so that chip fabrication and software drivers would not cause delays, and, over time, taking control of driver development back from the board makers. Intel launched a 3-D chip in 1998 but left the discrete graphics-chip business soon after, 3dfx's creditors started bankruptcy proceedings in 2000, and Forbes named Nvidia its Company of the Year in 2007. Rumelt adds a caution in a footnote: rivals such as ATI caught up later, so even a good strategy does not last forever.

Apple in 1997 is the example Postrel highlighted in Bloomberg View. When Steve Jobs returned, Apple was losing cash and selling a confusing, expensive range of products. In Rumelt's telling, Jobs's diagnosis was exactly that, and his guiding policy was to rebuild the business around a much simpler product line sold through fewer outlets. The coherent actions included cutting the product range sharply, moving most manufacturing to Taiwan, cutting software projects, dropping all but one national retailer, and opening an online store to sell directly. He also secured a 150-million-dollar investment from Microsoft and a commitment to keep making Mac software. Rumelt stresses what Jobs did not do: he did not announce ambitious revenue goals or a grand vision. When Rumelt met him in 1998 and asked about long-term strategy, Jobs said he was going to wait for the next big thing. Rumelt reads that as a real strategy for that moment: survive, stay coherent, and be ready to move when a technological window opens. In 2001 Apple opened its first retail stores and launched the iPod, followed by the iTunes Store in 2003 and the iPhone in 2007.

Walmart shows a different source of strength: insight. Conventional retail wisdom said each store should be managed as its own profit centre. Rumelt argues that Sam Walton's insight was to treat the integrated network of stores and distribution centres, not the individual store, as the operating unit. Clustering stores in small towns around a warehouse let Walmart serve places that rivals thought were too small, at costs that rivals could not match. The guiding policy and the actions followed from seeing the situation differently, not from working harder at the old model.

The smallest case is the most useful for a new venture. Rumelt describes a friend, Stephanie, who ran a corner grocery near a university and faced a large 24-hour supermarket nearby. Her diagnosis was that she could not beat the supermarket on range or price. Her guiding policy was to serve busy professionals who had little time to cook. The coherent actions were to stock more prepared meals and to open an extra checkout at 5 p.m. The strategy also told her what to stop doing. More prepared food meant less shelf space for snacks bought by students, and concentrating staff at the evening peak meant closing earlier and giving up late-night sales. That loss is the sign of a real choice.

sections.title: How the idea is used now, and its limits

blocks.text: Good Strategy/Bad Strategy became one of the most widely recommended strategy books of the 2010s, partly because its test is easy to use in a meeting. You can take any plan and ask three questions: what is the diagnosis, what is the guiding policy, and do the actions fit together? Many plans fail at the first question. In 2022 Rumelt followed up with The Crux, which focuses on finding the crux of a challenge, the part that is both most important and actually solvable.

The kernel fits well with other frameworks in this series. Five forces and the value chain help with diagnosis. Playing to Win's cascade of where to play and how to win is close to a guiding policy. Seven Powers describes the durable advantages that coherent actions can build. What Rumelt adds is a filter against self-deception: a reminder that a goal, a mission statement or a list of initiatives is not yet a strategy.

Critics note that the framework is easier to apply in hindsight than in advance. It is simple to call International Harvester's plan bad once the company has collapsed, and to call Nvidia's plan good once it has won. Rumelt's cases are also mostly his own retellings, and he says little about luck. The fair way to use the kernel is therefore as a discipline for your own thinking rather than as a way to grade other people's past decisions.

sections.title: Write a kernel for cool dairy

blocks.text: Write a one-page kernel for cool dairy, the vintage shop whose proceeds will support Taiwan women's organizations. Start with a diagnosis: what is the single most important obstacle right now? It might be finding enough good stock, getting buyers to trust a small shop, standing out on Carousell, or making the donation story credible. Then write one guiding policy that deals with that obstacle and rules some things out. Finally list three to five actions that reinforce each other. Like Stephanie's grocery, name at least one thing cool dairy will stop doing or will not do because of this choice. Then check your draft for Rumelt's four hallmarks: does it face the challenge, is it more than a goal, are the objectives few and reachable, and is there any fluff?

fun_fact.title: Action item 122: create a strategic plan
fun_fact.text: Rumelt once discussed strategy with the mayor of a small city in the US Pacific Northwest. The city's planning committee had produced a strategic plan with 47 strategies and 178 action items. Action item number 122 was 'create a strategic plan'. Rumelt uses it as his favourite example of the 'dog's dinner' style of bad strategy, where everything anyone suggested goes into the document and nothing is actually chosen.
